edits.why_correct: Smoking is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis, including peripheral arterial disease. It damages the endothelium, promotes plaque formation and increases the tendency to thrombosis. Stopping slows disease progression and reduces the risk of amputation, myocardial infarction and stroke. Source: NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease: diagnosis and management, 2012 (updated 2020).

issues: Accurate; thrombosis is the main complication of raised red cell mass (BSH 2019). Distinct from u74-g11 PAN4001 (hyperviscosity symptoms) and PAN4002 (ET). Fix: Source line and sources only.

edits.why_correct: An increased red cell mass raises haematocrit and whole-blood viscosity, slowing flow and promoting clot formation. This makes stroke, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis and unusual-site thromboses the major complications of erythrocytosis, particularly polycythaemia vera. Reducing the haematocrit by venesection is aimed mainly at lowering this risk. Source: British Society for Haematology guidelines on polycythaemia vera and secondary erythrocytosis, 2019.

edits.why_correct: With no reactive cause and a JAK2 mutation, this is essential thrombocythaemia, a myeloproliferative neoplasm. The excess platelets are often functionally abnormal, so patients are prone to arterial and venous thrombosis, yet very high counts can also cause bleeding through acquired von Willebrand syndrome. Both risks shape treatment decisions such as aspirin and cytoreduction. Source: British Committee for Standards in Haematology guideline for investigation and management of adults and children presenting with a thrombocytosis, 2010.

edits.why_correct: A persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit indicates an increased red cell concentration, which is polycythaemia (erythrocytosis). The extra red cells increase blood viscosity, causing headache, and the higher red cell content gives a plethoric, flushed face. It then needs evaluation for relative, secondary and primary causes. Source: British Society for Haematology guideline for the diagnosis and management of polycythaemia vera, 2019.
